mainEntity.name: Is sensitivity after composite bonding normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a degree of sensitivity following composite bonding is a commonly reported and well-recognised experience. The preparation of the tooth surface and the bonding process can temporarily stimulate the nerve, resulting in sensitivity to temperature, pressure, or sweet foods. For the majority of patients, this settles on its own within a few days to a few weeks. If sensitivity is severe, persistent, or accompanied by other symptoms, it is worth contacting your dental team for an assessment.

mainEntity.name: How long will sensitivity last after composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: For most patients, post-bonding sensitivity is most noticeable in the first 24 to 72 hours and then gradually reduces. The majority of patients find that sensitivity has resolved or significantly improved within two to four weeks. Individual timescales can vary depending on factors such as the extent of preparation involved, the number of teeth treated, and pre-existing dentine sensitivity. If sensitivity has not improved after four weeks, a dental review is recommended.

mainEntity.name: Can I use sensitivity toothpaste after composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, sensitivity toothpaste is generally considered appropriate for use following composite bonding and may help to ease temporary sensitivity during the recovery period. Toothpastes containing potassium nitrate or stannous fluoride are widely available and work by calming the response of the dentinal nerves over time. It is advisable to use it consistently as your regular toothpaste for several weeks to experience the full benefit. Your dental team can advise you on suitable products at your appointment.

mainEntity.name: Could sensitivity after composite bonding indicate a problem with the treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Sensitivity is a common physiological response to the composite bonding process and does not automatically indicate a treatment failure or complication. However, if sensitivity is particularly severe, is worsening rather than improving, occurs spontaneously without a trigger, or is accompanied by swelling or changes to the gum tissue, these are situations where a clinical assessment by your dental team would be appropriate. A professional review allows any concerns to be investigated properly.

mainEntity.name: How can I protect my composite bonding long-term?

acceptedAnswer.text: Maintaining good oral hygiene is central to protecting composite bonding restorations. This includes brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, using interdental brushes or floss daily, and attending regular dental check-ups and hygiene appointments. Avoiding habits such as nail biting, chewing on hard objects, or using your teeth as tools helps to reduce the risk of chipping. If you grind your teeth, discussing this with your dental team is important, as a custom night guard may help to protect the restorations. You can learn more on our cosmetic dentistry care advice page.

mainEntity.name: Will composite bonding sensitivity affect what I eat?

acceptedAnswer.text: During the immediate post-treatment period, it may be helpful to temporarily moderate your intake of very hot or very cold foods and drinks, as well as highly acidic or sugary items, to avoid unnecessary stimulation of the nerve. This is generally a short-term consideration rather than a long-term dietary restriction. Once sensitivity has resolved — which is typically within a few weeks — most patients return to a normal diet without difficulty. Your dental team can advise you on any specific dietary guidance relevant to your individual treatment.
